extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Greek tragedy / readers of Euripides' Electra (annotated edition)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading notes and commentary on Euripides' Electra focused on characterization, dramatic technique, choral function, mythic background, and moral/ritual implications in the play. Intended as guidance for interpreting and teaching this specific play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition through opening speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Electra's first two speeches are admirable as expositions of her character--the morbid nursing of hatred as a duty, the deliberate posing, the impulsiveness, the quick response to kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use opening speeches to reveal central traits (hatred as duty, posing, impulsiveness); judge how effectively they set up later actions and psychological conflicts (see commentary on pp. 5-6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed/traditional supporting characters (Pylades as persona muta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pylades is a persona muta ... a fixed traditional figure, possessing no quality but devotion to Orestes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and evaluate the function of stock/obligatory figures: they may lack individual development but serve as moral/plot anchors (compare Pylades' mute devotion here and his dramatic uses in other plays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local cultic and ritual detail to ground setting
rubrics_metrics.description: There seems to have been a priest born 'of the ancient folk' ... who, by some secret lore ... knew when Hera's festival was due, and walked round the country three days beforehand to announce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how ritual and cultic elements (e.g., the Watcher announcing Hera's festival) are used to create historical/religious verisimilitude and stage atmosphere; note any retained archaic practices and their dramatic implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character contrast and consistency (Electra's cowardice vs courage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe Electra's cowardice when surprised; contrast her courage, p. 47, when sending Orestes off, and again her quick drop to despair when the news does not come soon enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters by their range and internal contrasts: moments of apparent inconsistency may be deliberate to show emotional complexity (fear, devotion, despair) rather than poor characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of loyal servants/Old Man
rubrics_metrics.description: The Old Man, like other old family servants in Euripides ... is absolutely and even morbidly devoted to his masters. Delightful in this first scene, he becomes a little horrible in the next, where they plot the murders; not only ferocious himself, but, what seems worse, inclined to pet and enjoy the bloodthirstiness of his 'little mistress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge secondary characters by whether their loyalty is humanizing or disturbing; consider tonal shifts (from charming to horrible) and how they affect the audience's sympathy and the play's moral texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition signs should dramatize hope and denial
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole point of the scene requires that one ray of hope after another should be shown to Electra, and that she should passionately, blindly, reject them all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In recognition scenes, the signs (lock of hair, footprints, woven robe) must operate dramaturgically to build expectation and reveal psychological resistance; evaluate whether the handling achieves this emotional arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of canonical/traditional motifs (recognition signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because, whether invented by Aeschylus or not, these signs were a canonical part of the story by the time Euripides wrote. ... It would have been frivolous to invent new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an adaptation or retelling, account for the presence of longstanding story-elements as deliberate traditional motifs rather than mere borrowing; judge how faithfully and effectively an author uses canonical signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choral songs as 'embolima' (musical relief, not action-driving)
rubrics_metrics.description: The two main Choric songs of this play are markedly what Aristotle calls embolima 'things thrown in.' They have no effect upon the action, and form little more than musical 'relief.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the chorus by its function: determine whether it advances plot or provides lyrical/musical relief; consider appropriateness and effect of its placement and content (see pp. 28-30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythic backstory as thematic foundation (Golden Lamb as First Sin)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Golden Lamb. The theft of the Golden Lamb is treated as a story of the First Sin, after which all the world was changed and became the poor place that it now is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how mythic etiologies and ancestral crimes are used to frame the play's moral universe; judge whether such backstory clarifies or burdens the drama's themes (examples and speculative origins discussed pp. 47 ff.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Messenger-speech effectiveness and moral weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: This speech, though swift and vivid, is less moving and also less sympathetic than most of the Messengers' Speeches. Less moving, because the slaying of Aegisthus has little moral interest; it is merely a daring and dangerous exploit. Less sympathetic, because even here ... Euripides makes us feel the treacherous side of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique messenger reports by both craft (vividness, pace) and moral resonance; consider whether the reported act is framed as heroic or morally ambivalent and how that framing affects audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural norms for treatment of the dead inform moral judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat the dead with respect was one of the special marks of a Greek as opposed to a barbarian. ... Any excess of this kind, any violence towards the helpless, was apt to rouse 'The sleeping wrath of the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating scenes of killing and postmortem treatment, factor in contemporary (Greek) ethical norms and the likely audience reaction; excesses may be judged as violations inviting cosmic/choral retribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical status of revenge depends on ritual/guest relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If Orestes had washed with Aegisthus, he would have become his xenos, or guest, as much as if he had eaten his bread and salt. In that case the slaying would have been definitely a crime, a dishonourable act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess vengeance scenes with attention to ritual markers (guest-friendship, hospitality rituals, clothing/washing) that alter the moral valence of killing; such ritual detail can convert a 'just' reprisal into dishonourable murder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of motive: mixture of personal resentment and filial devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe the mixture of all sorts of personal resentments and jealousies with the devotion of the lonely woman to her father and her brother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate protagonists by mapping overlapping motives (self-interest, jealousy, duty) rather than seeking single explanations; recognize that mixtures of motives enhance tragic plausibility and dramatic tension.
